title: Getting Started (Computer System Basics and Architectures)
learningGoals: Name the basic parts of a computer system and explain what each one does.
Explain the memory hierarchy (registers → L1 → L2 → L3 → main memory → disk) and why data moves in blocks.
Explain the stored program concept (von Neumann), and the Harvard and Modified Harvard architectures, with their merits and demerits.
Explain multi-core cache behaviour: look-through vs look-aside and write-update vs write-invalidate.
Classify multiprocessor systems (tightly vs loosely coupled, homogeneous vs heterogeneous, NUMA vs NORMA).
Tell i3, i5, i7 and i9 apart by technology (hyper-threading, turbo boost), and explain why lower frequency saves power (P ∝ V²·F·C).
sirStressed: Think in systems, not parts. Focus on application and reasoning, not memorisation. Recorded videos teach the WHAT; live sessions teach the WHY and HOW.
RAM is volatile: power off and its contents are gone. Storage is persistent.
A core = registers (CPU state) + interrupt logic + execution unit + cache. Hardware threads are counted by register sets.

Hyper-threading ≠ two cores. HT gives two register sets but one execution unit, so only one task runs at a time and the gain comes from fast switching when a task waits. Two cores really run two tasks in parallel, provided they don't depend on each other.
Interrupts: like a student interrupting the lecture with a doubt, an important event interrupts the CPU, and the interrupt logic handles it.
Use tools like the Intel identification utility or CPU-Z to see your own cores, threads and cache.
commonTraps: "Harvard is the most used architecture." Wrong. Modified Harvard is (split L1 only).
Mixing up look-through (sequential, standard) with look-aside (parallel, faster on a miss, but cancellation signals make it rare).
Picking write-update when the question says "repeated writes to the same block". The answer is write-invalidate.
Thinking hyper-threading means two programs execute at the same instant. It doesn't: there is one execution unit.
NUMA vs NORMA: NORMA = no remote memory access (loosely coupled, message passing). NUMA = non-uniform (tightly coupled, shared memory).
Saying a processor group is "homogeneous" without saying at which level (ISA or frequency).
Assuming a program can run directly from disk. The stored program concept says it must be in memory.
Treating keyboard and mouse as block devices. They're character devices; disks and SSDs are block devices.
summary: System = CPU (ALU + control unit + registers) + memory subsystem (L1/L2/L3/RAM) + I/O, with storage as secondary memory.
Hierarchy: smaller = faster. Inclusive (L1 ⊂ L2 ⊂ L3 ⊂ RAM). Transfers are blocks (different sizes per level), and L1↔CPU moves words. Blocks exist because of locality of reference.
von Neumann / stored program: programs and data are in memory and execute from memory. Bottleneck: a unified cache can't serve fetch and data access together under pipelining.
Harvard: split I/D caches at all levels, which helps pipelining. But no balancing and no on-the-fly instruction modification.
Modified Harvard: split L1, unified L2 and below. Gets the best of both, and it's used today.
Multi-core: private split L1 per core, shared unified L2/L3. On an L1 miss, search the other L1s first. Look-through is the standard; look-aside is faster but needs cancellation signals.
Coherence: write-invalidate for many writes, write-update for few writes.
Multiprocessor: tightly coupled (shared memory, NUMA; homogeneous at ISA or frequency level, or heterogeneous) vs loosely coupled (network, message passing, NORMA).
Intel: i3 = HT, i5 = turbo, i7 = HT + turbo, i9 = multiple turbo levels. P ∝ V²FC, so lower V and F save power.
HT vs cores: HT duplicates registers and interrupt logic only; a core duplicates everything.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an I/O device?
questions.explanation: a joystick is an input device. L1/L2 caches and ROM are all part of the memory subsystem.
topicTags: Basic Components of a Computer System

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a part of the memory subsystem?
questions.explanation: the memory subsystem is registers, caches and main memory. Pen drives and hard disks are secondary storage (I/O), and a keyboard is input.
topicTags: Basic Components of a Computer System

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is NOT a part of the memory subsystem?
questions.explanation: a hard disk is secondary memory, treated as an I/O device, not part of the CPU-side memory hierarchy.
topicTags: Basic Components of a Computer System

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is TRUE in the von Neumann architecture?

options.text: Programs can be executed directly from the hard disk
Programs should reside in memory for execution
Programs can be executed both from memory and from the hard disk
Programs can be executed directly from I/O devices

questions.explanation: stored-program concept. A program must be loaded into main memory before the CPU can execute it.
topicTags: Unicore Systems with Stored Program Concept

questions.prompt: Which of the following designs are NOT possible in the von Neumann architecture? (more than one answer)
questions.explanation: with one unified memory/cache, an instruction fetch and a data access can't happen in the same cycle. Pipelining and superscalar designs need exactly that.
topicTags: Unicore Systems with Stored Program Concept

questions.prompt: What is the main organisational change in the Harvard architecture over von Neumann?

options.text: L1 is split (instruction/data) and all other levels are unified
All cache levels are split into instruction and data caches
L2 is split and the other levels are unified

questions.explanation: in Harvard, instructions and data follow completely separate paths at every level.

questions.prompt: What is the main organisational change in the Modified Harvard architecture over von Neumann? (same options)

options.text: L1 is split (instruction/data) and all other levels are unified
All cache levels are split into instruction and data caches
L2 is split and the other levels are unified

questions.explanation: only L1 is split, for parallel fetch and data access. Lower levels stay unified so instructions can be modified on the fly.

questions.prompt: What is the main organisational change in Modified Harvard over Harvard? (same options)

options.text: L1 is split (instruction/data) and all other levels are unified
All cache levels are split into instruction and data caches
L2 is split and the other levels are unified

questions.explanation: compared with Harvard, modified Harvard keeps the split only at L1 and unifies L2 and below.

questions.prompt: Which cache module is local to the core?
questions.explanation: each core has its own private split L1. L2/L3 are shared.

questions.prompt: If a local L1 miss occurs in a multi-core system, from which cache is the data transferred?
questions.explanation: the other cores' L1s are checked first, because they may hold the latest (modified) copy. That's how coherence is kept.

questions.prompt: The Intel Atom processor is an example of a ______ multiprocessor system.
questions.explanation: all of Atom's cores run the same ISA (x86) but can run at different frequencies, which makes it ISA-level symmetric.

questions.prompt: Which one is NOT a loosely coupled multiprocessor system?
questions.explanation: NUMA is tightly coupled (shared memory). The others communicate over a network (message passing, NORMA).

questions.prompt: Which Intel processor has 2 turbo-boosting frequencies?
questions.explanation: the lecture: i5 has turbo, i7 has HT + turbo, and i9 has multiple turbo levels (Turbo Boost 2.0 + Turbo Boost Max 3.0). worked out, not from the quiz review.

questions.prompt: Which Intel processor does NOT support hyper-threading?
questions.explanation: in the lecture's comparison, i3 = HT without turbo, i5 = turbo without HT, and i7/i9 = both. worked out, not from the quiz review.

questions.prompt: Which architecture do most modern laptop processors follow?
questions.explanation: Modified Harvard: split L1 (I and D), unified L2 and below.

questions.prompt: In a Harvard architecture, which of these is a demerit?

options.text: Instructions cannot be modified on the fly
Instructions and data share one cache

questions.explanation: Instructions and data are fully separated, so you can't modify an instruction on the fly. (Harvard helps pipelining, so (a) is wrong.)

questions.prompt: Core C1 is going to write to the same cache block 50 times in a row. Another core has a copy. Which policy is preferred?
questions.explanation: Write-invalidate. Invalidate once and after that only C1 holds the block, so the later writes cost nothing extra. Write-update would broadcast all 50 writes.

questions.prompt: A cache access scheme that signals the next level at the same time as searching the current level is called:
questions.explanation: Look-aside. It's faster on a miss but needs cancellation signals, so look-through is the standard.

questions.prompt: Ten processors share the same ISA; nine run at 3.6 GHz and one at 4.2 GHz. The system is:

options.text: Homogeneous at ISA and frequency level

questions.explanation: Same ISA means ISA-level homogeneous. Different frequencies mean not frequency-level homogeneous.

questions.prompt: The memory model of a loosely coupled multiprocessor (for example, client-server over a network) is:
questions.explanation: NORMA, No Remote Memory Access. Nodes communicate only by message passing.

questions.prompt: State the stored program concept in one or two lines.
correctAnswers: Everything the CPU executes, both instructions and data, must reside in main memory. A program is loaded from storage into memory before it runs.
questions.explanation: Everything the CPU executes, both instructions and data, must reside in main memory. A program is loaded from storage into memory before it runs.

questions.prompt: Why is data moved between memory levels in blocks rather than single bytes?
correctAnswers: Because of locality of reference: after accessing item i, items next to it (i+1, …) are likely to be needed soon, so bringing the whole block avoids future misses.
questions.explanation: Because of locality of reference: after accessing item i, items next to it (i+1, …) are likely to be needed soon, so bringing the whole block avoids future misses.

questions.prompt: A CPU drops from 1.0 V and 3 GHz to 0.8 V and 1.5 GHz. By what factor does dynamic power change?
correctAnswers: (0.8/1.0)² × (1.5/3) = 0.64 × 0.5 = 0.32. Power falls to about 32% of the original.
questions.explanation: (0.8/1.0)² × (1.5/3) = 0.64 × 0.5 = 0.32. Power falls to about 32% of the original.

questions.prompt: Explain how hyper-threading differs from having two cores.
correctAnswers: HT adds an extra register set and interrupt logic to one core with one execution unit, so two threads are loaded but only one executes at a time, and the core switches quickly when one waits. Two cores each have their own execution unit, so two independent threads really run in parallel.
questions.explanation: HT adds an extra register set and interrupt logic to one core with one execution unit, so two threads are loaded but only one executes at a time, and the core switches quickly when one waits. Two cores each have their own execution unit, so two independent threads really run in parallel.
